claims.text: Controlled nanoscale precipitation introduced by thermomechanical processing will improve the combination of strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional single-phase HEAs.
The proposed initial material is a homogenized, single-phase HEA, typically with an FCC or BCC structure.
Cold or warm deformation followed by aging will induce nanoscale precipitate formation in the HEA matrix.
Processing must avoid excessive grain growth or embrittlement for the proposed benefit to occur.
The alloy composition must permit secondary-phase precipitation without destabilizing the matrix.
The processing route will produce nanoscale precipitates dispersed in the matrix and thereby create a dual-phase microstructure.
The precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion and increase strength.
A nanoscale precipitate size and suitable distribution will permit dislocation bypass and preserve ductility.
The dual-phase structure will impede crack propagation and enhance fracture resistance.
A precipitate phase stiffer than the matrix may increase Young's modulus.
Yield strength will increase by at least 20% relative to the single-phase baseline.
Fracture toughness will increase by at least 20% relative to the single-phase baseline.
Ductility will be maintained or improved, with total elongation exceeding 15%.
Young's modulus may increase by 5-10% relative to the single-phase baseline.
A typical single-phase HEA baseline has a yield strength of approximately 600 MPa.
A typical single-phase HEA baseline has a fracture toughness of approximately 60 MPa·m^0.5.
A typical single-phase HEA baseline has a Young's modulus of approximately 120 GPa.
A typical single-phase HEA baseline has an elongation to failure of approximately 10-15%.
Coarse precipitates or continuous precipitate networks may cause embrittlement and reduce ductility and fracture resistance.
If the matrix composition does not support precipitation, the proposed improvement will not occur.
